claims.text: The test particles are initially solid, chemically homogeneous, sub-10 nm Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles possess significant intrinsic lattice strain due to atomic-size mismatch.
Local atomic segregation predominantly governs the premelting and melting behavior of Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles.
Atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice strain predominantly governs the premelting and melting behavior of Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles.
Restricted atomic mobility during heating contributes to the formation of segregated, defect-rich regions.
Atomic-size mismatch produces built-in lattice strain in the HEA nanoparticles.
Limited atomic mobility during heating prevents complete atomic mixing.
Segregated and defect-rich regions initiate premelting below the bulk melting temperature.
Spatially localized premelting broadens the overall melting transition.
Local segregation and lattice strain promote surface disorder and localized premelting.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a lower premelting onset than comparable single-metal or binary-alloy nanoparticles.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a broader and more gradual melting transition than comparable single-metal or binary-alloy nanoparticles.
Early loss of crystallinity and increased surface disorder will accompany the predicted premelting behavior.
Single-metal or binary-alloy baseline nanoparticles have more uniform atomic structures.
Single-metal or binary-alloy baseline nanoparticles exhibit sharper and more uniform melting transitions.
Rapid cooling can preserve a single-solid-solution, high-entropy nanoparticle state by suppressing secondary-phase formation.
The proposed premelting mechanism applies to sub-10 nm particles synthesized under rapid-cooling, nonequilibrium conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to larger particles or particles produced under equilibrium conditions.
